summary: This Standards Track document describes DMARC failure reports, which give details about individual messages that failed to authenticate under DMARC. It updates RFC 6591 and obsoletes RFC 7489.

plainLanguage.summary: DMARC lets the owner of an email domain ask receiving servers to report mail that failed the domain's checks. This RFC defines the detailed report: one per failed message, sent almost at once, rather than a daily total. The report can carry the failed message's headers and body, which is useful for finding out what went wrong but also exposes personal data, so many providers turn it off.

questions: what is a dmarc failure report
what is the ruf tag in dmarc
subtitle: Per-message DMARC failure reports that tell a domain owner exactly which mail failed authentication.

tldr.problem: Aggregate DMARC reports give totals but not the details of a particular failed message, which makes it hard to find the cause of a failure or spot direct abuse of a domain quickly.
tldr.mechanism: A Mail Receiver sends a failure report in the RFC 6591 abuse report format shortly after a DMARC failure, to the addresses in the ruf tag. RFC 9991 adds an Identity-Alignment field and a dmarc Auth-Failure type.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9991 updates RFC 6591 and, with RFC 9989 and RFC 9990, obsoletes RFC 7489. It warns that reports can expose personal data, and many large providers limit or disable them.

today: RFC 9991 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. It updates RFC 6591 and, together with RFC 9989 and RFC 9990, obsoletes RFC 7489. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) is a mechanism by which a mail-originating organization can express domain-level policies and preferences for message validation, disposition and reporting, which a mail-receiving organization can use to improve mail handling. This document focuses on one type of reporting that can be requested under DMARC.

Failure reports provide detailed information about the failure of a single message or a group of similar messages failing for the same reason. Their purpose is twofold. On the one hand, they are meant to aid cases where a Domain Owner wishes to determine the cause of failures that were part of aggregate reports. On the other hand, they can allow the Domain Owner to quickly identify and address harmful messages involving direct domain abuse.

The document notes that these reports can contain the header fields or sometimes the entire content of a failed message, which may contain Personally Identifiable Information (PII). The potential disclosure of PII should be considered when deciding whether to request failure reports as a Domain Owner, what information to include or redact when creating them as a Mail Receiver, or whether to create failure reports at all.

The format of DMARC failure reports is derived from the abuse reporting format document, and the terms defined there are used here.
sections.plainLanguage: A failure report is about one message, or a group of messages that failed for the same reason. It exists to help a domain owner work out why a message failed the checks, and to spot abuse of the domain quickly. The catch is that a report can carry the failed message itself, which may hold personal information.

sections.title: DMARC Failure Reports
sections.content:
Besides the header fields or the entire contents of a failed message, failure reports supply details about transmission and DMARC authentication, which may aid a Domain Owner in determining the cause of an authentication failure.

Failure reports are normally generated and sent almost immediately after the Mail Receiver detects a DMARC failure, rather than waiting for an aggregate report. This makes them useful for quickly notifying Domain Owners when there is an authentication failure, and they provide more information about the failed message than an aggregate report does. That allows the consumer of the report to tell whether the failure is of a message the Domain Owner intended to authenticate or one for which use of its domain was not authorized. These reports should include as much of the message header fields and body as possible, consistent with the reporting party's privacy policies, to enable the Domain Owner to diagnose the failure.

When a Domain Owner requests failure reports for the purpose of forensic analysis, and the Mail Receiver is willing to provide such reports, the Mail Receiver generates and sends a message using the format described in the abuse reporting format document. The destinations to which failure reports are sent, and options for when they will be sent, are defined by the ruf and fo tags.

When multiple Uniform Resource Identifiers are provided to receive failure reports, the report generator MUST make an attempt to deliver to each of them. External destinations MUST be verified. Report generators MUST NOT consider ruf tags in DMARC Policy Records that have a psd=y tag, unless there are specific agreements between the interested parties. Report generators MUST implement a rate-limit on outgoing reports so as not to flood Report Consumers with excessive reports, which would allow denial of service.

The document also covers other failure reports. DKIM failure reports and SPF failure reports are described separately. A Mail Receiver that generates DMARC failure reports MAY choose to issue failure reports of the type specific to the authentication mechanism that failed instead of, or in addition to, the DMARC failure report type described here. The Receiver SHALL determine which failure report types, if any, to transmit based on its own policy, the failure in question and the content of the fo tag in the retrieved DMARC Policy Record.
sections.plainLanguage: The report goes out almost at once, not at the end of the day, and it carries more detail than a daily summary does, so the domain owner can tell a broken message of their own from one that was sent in their name without permission. Reports go to the addresses in the ruf tag, each one is tried, and the sender of the report must limit how many it sends.

sections.title: Reporting Format Update
sections.content:
Operators implementing this specification also implement an augmented version of the abuse reporting format. A DMARC failure report includes the following Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) header fields, with the indicated normative requirement levels.

  • Identity-Alignment (REQUIRED; defined below)
  • Delivery-Result (OPTIONAL)
  • DKIM-Domain, DKIM-Identity, DKIM-Selector (REQUIRED for DKIM failures of an aligned identifier)
  • DKIM-Canonicalized-Header, DKIM-Canonicalized-Body (OPTIONAL if reporting a DKIM failure)
  • SPF-DNS (REQUIRED for SPF failure of an aligned identifier)

The Identity-Alignment field is defined to contain a comma-separated list of authentication mechanism names that failed to authenticate an aligned identity, or the keyword none if all of the attempted methods were successful at authenticating an aligned identity. The ABNF is:

id-align     = "Identity-Alignment:" [CFWS]
                 ( "none" /
                   dmarc-method
                     *( [CFWS] "," [CFWS] dmarc-method ) )
                 [CFWS]

dmarc-method = ( "dkim" / "spf" )
               ; each may appear at most once in an id-align

An Authentication Failure Type of dmarc is defined for the Auth-Failure field, which is to be used when a failure report is generated because some or all of the authentication mechanisms failed to produce aligned identifiers. A failure report generator MAY also independently produce an ARF message for any or all of the underlying authentication methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The one new required field is Identity-Alignment. It lists the checks that failed to line up with the domain, dkim or spf, or says none when they all did. The Auth-Failure field gains a new value, dmarc, for reports caused by a failure to produce an aligned identifier.

sections.title: Verifying External Destinations
sections.content:
It is possible to specify destinations for failure reports that are outside of the Organizational Domain of the DMARC Policy Record that was requesting the reports. These destinations are commonly referred to as external destinations, and may represent a different domain controlled by the same organization, a contracted report processing service, or some other arrangement.

In case of external destinations, a Mail Receiver who generates failure reports MUST use the Verifying External Destinations procedure described in the aggregate reporting document, substituting the ruf tag where the rua tag appears in that procedure.

This prevents a bad actor from publishing a DMARC Policy Record requesting failure reports to an external destination and then deliberately sending messages that will generate failure reports as a form of abuse. It also prevents a Domain Owner from unilaterally publishing a DMARC Policy Record with an external destination for failure reports, forcing the external destination to deal with unwanted messages and potential privacy issues.

Email streams carrying DMARC failure reports SHOULD be DMARC-aligned. The document recommends that reporters set a reasonable rate-limit for the number of failure reports sent to any recipient to avoid overloading recipient systems, because unaligned reports may in turn produce subsequent failure reports that could cause mail loops.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain can point its reports at an address outside its own organisation, such as a contractor that processes them. Before sending anywhere, the sending server has to check that the destination really belongs to the domain, so that a domain cannot aim a flood of reports at someone else.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has updated the reference and description for the Identity-Alignment entry in the Feedback Report Header Fields registry within the Messaging Abuse Reporting Format Parameters registry group.

  • Field Name: Identity-Alignment
  • Description: a list of authentication mechanism names that failed to authenticate an aligned identity, or none if all were successful
  • Multiple Appearances: No
  • Related Feedback-Type: auth-failure
  • Reference: RFC 9991
  • Status: current
sections.plainLanguage: IANA's registry entry for the new field points at this RFC and describes what it holds. The field may appear only once in a report and belongs to the auth-failure report type.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The generation and transmission of DMARC failure reports raise significant privacy concerns that must be carefully considered before deployment. Given these factors, many large-scale providers limit or entirely disable the generation of failure reports, preferring to rely on aggregate reports, which provide statistical visibility without exposing sensitive content. Operators that choose to enable failure reporting are strongly encouraged to limit the scope and duration of use to targeted diagnostic activities, to ensure that reporting URIs are carefully controlled and validated, to apply minimization techniques such as redaction of message bodies and header fields, and always to transmit reports over secure channels. Aggregate reports remain the recommended mechanism for gaining visibility into authentication results while preserving the confidentiality of end-user communications.

On data exposure, failure reports may include PII and non-public information (NPI) from messages that fail to authenticate, since these reports may contain message content as well as trace header fields. They may expose sender and recipient identifiers, and although the failed-message reporting format supports redaction, failed-message reporting is capable of exposing the entire message to the Report Consumer. Examples of what may leak include product launches, termination notices for employees, or calendar data. Even innocuous-seeming failures, such as malformed or broken calendar invitations, can result in the leakage of private communications.

Domain Owners requesting reports will receive information about mail using their domain, but which they did not actually cause to be sent. This might provide valuable insight into content used in abusive messages, but it might also expose PII or NPI from legitimate messages that failed authentication by mistake. Information about the final destination of mail, where it might otherwise be obscured by intermediate systems, may be exposed through a failure report. A commonly cited example is exposure of members of mailing lists when one list member sends messages to the list and failure reports are generated when that message is delivered to other list members. Similarly, when message forwarding arrangements exist, destinations previously unknown to the Domain Owner may become visible.

A DMARC Policy Record can specify that reports should be sent to a Report Consumer operating on behalf of the Domain Owner, for example to monitor mail streams for deliverability, performance issues or abuse. Receipt of such data by third parties may or may not be permitted by the Mail Receiver's privacy policy or terms of use, so Domain Owners and Mail Receivers should both review whether their own internal policies constrain the use and transmission of DMARC reporting. Some potential exists for Report Consumers to perform traffic analysis, making it possible to obtain metadata about the Mail Receiver's traffic.

The risks associated with failure reports are compounded by volume and content distribution concerns. Partially or unredacted reports may propagate large amounts of spam, phishing or malware content. Report generators are asked to help prevent accidental access to potentially malicious URIs by substituting hxxp for http, and to remove attachments that could embed malicious payload. Report consumers are asked to isolate report streams from other mail streams, to use sandboxes in evaluating failure reports, to use network segmentation, and to limit access to failure reports to authorized individuals with appropriate security training.
sections.plainLanguage: These reports can carry the failed message, so they can leak personal data, confidential business information and even the addresses on a mailing list. The document therefore asks for redaction, controlled reporting addresses, secure channels and rate limits, and it notes that many large providers have switched the whole thing off and rely on aggregate reports instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
While reviewing this document and its security considerations, the reader should also review the privacy considerations above, as well as the privacy considerations and security considerations in the DMARC and aggregate reporting documents.

Failure reports represent a possible denial-of-service attack that could be perpetrated by an attacker who sends numerous messages purporting to be from the intended victim Domain Owner but which fail both SPF and DKIM. This would cause participating Mail Receivers to send failure reports to the Domain Owner or its delegates, potentially in large numbers. Participating Mail Receivers are therefore encouraged to aggregate these reports as much as is practical, using the Incidents field of the ARF. The aim is not to count each and every failure but rather to report different failure conditions.

Various pruning techniques are possible. A receiver can store reports for a period of time before sending them, which allows detection, collection and consolidation of like incidents. It can also apply rate-limiting, such as a maximum number of reports per minute that will be generated, with the remainder discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The obvious attack is to send a flood of messages in the victim's name, so that every receiving server sends a failure report to the victim. Receivers are asked to group reports together and to cap how many they send per minute.

sections.title: Example Failure Report
sections.content:
The appendix gives the full content of a sample failure message, including the message header. The report itself is the MIME part with the content type message/feedback-report, and it carries these fields:

Feedback-Type: auth-failure
Version: 1
User-Agent: DMARC-Filter/1.2.3
Auth-Failure: dmarc
Authentication-Results: gen.example;
  dmarc=fail header.from=consumer.example
Identity-Alignment: dkim
DKIM-Domain: consumer.example
DKIM-Identity: @consumer.example
DKIM-Selector: epsilon
Original-Envelope-Id: 65E1A3F0A0
Original-Mail-From: author=gen.example@forwarder.example
Source-IP: 192.0.2.2
Source-Port: 12345
Reported-Domain: consumer.example

The Source-Port field definition is given by the source ports document. In the final MIME entity, the local parts of To and From addresses are reported unredacted. Since the local parts are known to be PII, the privacy risk can be reduced by redacting them: in the example, the report generator could have replaced users with lRLxexey and author with RT47aVey throughout the entity. If the body of the message is not included, the last MIME entity would have the content type text/rfc822-headers instead of message/rfc822.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows a complete report for one failed message. It names the domain that was misused, the address the mail came from, and which check failed to line up, and it then carries the original message so the domain owner can look at it.
